source_title: Physical and Constructive Invasion of Privacy (drone-inclusive)
regulated_activity: Capturing (or attempting to capture, by any device) an image/recording of a person engaging in a private, personal, or familial activity in an offensive manner
summary: Civil Code § 1708.8 creates civil liability for (a) 'physical invasion of privacy' — knowingly entering the land or airspace above another's land without permission, or otherwise trespassing, to capture an image/recording of a person engaging in private, personal, or familial activity in an offensive manner — and (b) 'constructive invasion of privacy' — using any device, including a drone, to attempt such a capture in an offensive manner where the capture could not have been achieved without a trespass but for use of the device, regardless of physical trespass. Liability is up to 3x general/special damages plus possible punitive damages and disgorgement of commercial proceeds; a separate civil fine of $5,000-$50,000 applies for a commercial-purpose violation. Subdivision (g) exempts law-enforcement and governmental-agency personnel acting within the course of an authorized investigation supported by articulable suspicion. 'Private, personal, and familial activity' is defined in subdivision (l), generally requiring a reasonable expectation of privacy.
practical_interpretation_aec_expert: Even without physically trespassing, capturing offensive/private imagery via drone that could only have been obtained through trespass but for the device can trigger 'constructive invasion of privacy' liability — plan flight paths and camera framing on AEC projects to avoid capturing identifiable people engaged in private activity on adjoining residential parcels.
practical_interpretation_uas_procurement: N/A — no procurement or equipment-selection implication identified
practical_interpretation_legal_counsel: This is a civil tort with treble damages, punitive damages, and a $5,000-$50,000 statutory civil fine exposure — document the professional purpose of any flight capturing imagery near residential property, and consider blurring/redaction workflows for incidentally captured individuals on adjoining private property.
verification_status: Full section text pulled directly from Justia's codification of the current California Civil Code; amendment history (Stats. 2015 Ch. 521, AB 856) confirmed in the statute's own history line.

source_title: Remaining at Scene of Emergency to Impede Personnel (drone-inclusive)
regulated_party: Any person (expressly including a remote drone operator regardless of the operator's physical location)
regulated_activity: Operating/using a UAS at the scene of an emergency in a manner that impedes police, fire, EMS, or military personnel performing emergency duties
summary: It is a misdemeanor to go to or stop at the scene of an emergency to view the activities of emergency personnel and thereby impede those personnel, unless viewing the scene is part of the person's job duties. Subdivision (a)(2), added in 2016, expressly extends the section to 'a person, regardless of his or her location, who operates or uses an unmanned aerial vehicle, remote piloted aircraft, or drone that is at the scene of an emergency' — meaning the remote pilot need not be physically present at the scene to be liable. 'Emergency' is broadly defined to include fires, explosions, crashes, flooding, windstorm damage, railroad/traffic accidents, powerplant accidents, and toxic/biological spills.
practical_interpretation_aec_expert: Treat active fire, crash, or disaster scenes as an automatic no-fly for any AEC UAS mission (e.g., post-event damage/infrastructure documentation) until coordinating directly with incident command — CAL FIRE and other agencies actively enforce this provision and a remote pilot can be liable even when not physically on scene.
practical_interpretation_uas_procurement: N/A — no procurement or equipment-selection implication identified
practical_interpretation_legal_counsel: Document incident-command coordination and any professional/job-duty basis for flying near an active emergency before tasking a crew; the person's-job-duties exception is narrow and does not automatically cover general infrastructure-damage assessment work absent an agency request or authorization.
verification_status: Full section text pulled directly from Justia's codification, including the 2016 drone-specific amendment (AB 1680) reflected in the statute's history line.

source_title: Prohibition on Using Aircraft (Including Drones) to Pursue or Harass Wildlife
regulated_activity: Using a UAS (or other aircraft/device capable of flight) to pursue, drive, herd, take, or harass game/nongame birds or mammals; locating big-game mammals within 48 hours of a big-game season
summary: 14 CCR Section 251 prohibits pursuing, driving, herding, or taking any bird or mammal from a motor-driven air vehicle, and separately bars using any motorized, hot-air, or unpowered aircraft or other flight-capable device (including an earth-orbiting imaging device) to locate or assist in locating big-game mammals from 48 hours before through 48 hours after any big-game season. 14 CCR Section 251.1 separately prohibits harassing (defined as an intentional act disrupting an animal's normal behavior patterns, including breeding, feeding, or sheltering) any game or nongame bird, mammal, or furbearing mammal by drone or otherwise.
practical_interpretation_aec_expert: Plan environmental-monitoring, habitat-mapping, or resource-inventory UAS flights to avoid disrupting normal wildlife behavior (breeding, feeding, sheltering) and avoid any use that could be read as locating big-game animals near a hunting season window.

permit_or_approval_required: Yes — permit type depends on the nature of the operation
summary: Drones are generally allowed in State Parks, State Beaches, State Historic Parks, State Recreation Areas, and State Vehicular Recreation Areas except where prohibited by a District Superintendent's posted order (issued for reasons such as species protection, cultural/natural resource protection, fire danger, public safety, or visitor-experience/privacy concerns) — drone users should always check with the local State Park District for unit-specific posted orders. Commercial drone use additionally requires a permit; commercial operators must submit their FAA authorization to the relevant State Park District, and depending on the proposed use the District Superintendent may require a Special Event permit, Right of Entry permit, or other approval; commercial photography/filming within a state park separately requires a California Film Commission permit (14 CCR Section 4316). Research UAS use requires FAA approval and a submitted copy to the District, plus a DPR 65 scientific collection permit for any scientific research/survey. Public-agency UAS use requires submission of the operator's FAA Certificate of Waiver or Authorization (COA) to the District.

source_title: Encroachment Permit Requirement for UAS Operations Within the State Highway System Right-of-Way

regulated_party: Any person launching, landing, or operating a UAS from within the State Highway System right-of-way
regulated_activity: Launching, landing, or operating a UAS within Caltrans right-of-way, or entering the right-of-way to conduct UAS-related activities
summary: Operating a UAS from within the State Highway System (SHS) right-of-way requires a Caltrans encroachment permit; this applies before launching, landing, or entering the SHS right-of-way to operate or participate in UAS-related activities, regardless of where the remote pilot, visual observer, or support personnel are physically located or where the aircraft is actually flown. Encroachment permit requests are considered only when associated with authorized construction work or other permitted activities such as commercial filming, special events, surveys, or accident reconstruction; UAS operations for recreational, private, or general business purposes are not allowed within the SHS right-of-way. Caltrans contractors/consultants must additionally coordinate UAS use on current Caltrans projects with the Division of Aeronautics and the project's Caltrans contract/project coordinator. Caltrans notes the FAA has exclusive regulatory authority over UAS operations and civilian airspace, but the encroachment permit is a separate, additional state/property-access requirement.
practical_interpretation_aec_expert: For any highway/bridge corridor survey, mapping, or inspection project, submit the Standard Encroachment Permit Application (TR-0100) to the local District Encroachment Permits Office well before mobilization, and separately coordinate with the Division of Aeronautics and the Caltrans project/contract coordinator on Caltrans-scoped task orders.

practical_interpretation_legal_counsel: Confirm the encroachment permit is in hand — not merely applied for — before authorizing any launch, landing, or right-of-way entry for UAS purposes; document that the underlying activity (survey, construction-related work, accident reconstruction) fits within the categories Caltrans will actually consider for a permit, since recreational/general business UAS use in the right-of-way is categorically excluded.

regulated_party: Licensed land surveyors (and by extension, those performing surveying-equivalent work)
regulated_activity: Determining the configuration or contour of the earth's surface, or the position of fixed objects, by applying mathematics or photogrammetry
summary: A person practices land surveying within the meaning of the Land Surveyors Act if they determine the configuration or contour of the earth's surface, or the position of fixed objects above, on, or below the surface, by applying the principles of mathematics or photogrammetry, in a public or private capacity. The statute separately defines 'geodetic surveying' and 'cadastral surveying.' BPELSG's general competency rule additionally requires a licensed PE or PLS to practice only in fields in which they are, by education and/or experience, fully competent and proficient — a rule industry commentary treats as especially applicable to UAS-derived mapping.
practical_interpretation_aec_expert: Because photogrammetric determination of ground configuration/contour falls within the statutory definition of land surveying, route UAS-derived photogrammetry or LiDAR mapping products intended to establish configuration, contour, or fixed-object position through a California-licensed PLS (or PE where applicable) rather than treating it as unregulated general mapping.

practical_interpretation_legal_counsel: Confirm whether a given UAS-derived deliverable crosses from general imagery/documentation into 'determining the configuration or contour of the earth's surface' as statutorily defined — that determination controls whether PLS licensure is required — and document licensed-professional review in the QA/QC record for any deliverable that does.
